newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Political normality creeps back in south Albania.
newsitem.headline: Political normality creeps back in south Albania.

text.p: The town of Vlore, the southern hotbed of Albania's recent anarchy, witnessed its first peaceful political event in months on Monday as opposition socialists mounted an election rally in the town.

A crowd of 6,000-8,000 people turned out to cheer Socialist party chairman Fatos Nano and other Socialist and Social Democratic Party leaders, campaigning for the June 29 general election on the town's dusty main square.

The rally was the first in an opposition tour this week of the southern towns, some of which have spun out of government control since anarchy and unrest swept Albania after the collapse of fraudulent savings schemes early this year.
Police and the party's own security forces provided tight security for the meeting, which took place just days after regular uniformed police started to reappear on Vlore's streets.
For some weeks they had been scarcely visible following a flare-up in gang warfare after a local police chief resigned.
Flags fluttered in stifling heat as supporters cheered and chanted amid the wrecked and unfinished buildings on the square, mobbing Nano when he arrived.
A young woman embraced him and wished him success. "We expected you to visit a long time ago, we are very happy with your arrival," she said.

Nano, looking relaxed, promised to find a way to get back money people had lost in the fraudulent schemes. He called a minute's silence to honour the 150 or so citizens of the town killed in rioting earlier this year.

The rally came a day after officials at the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE), preparing to bring foreign observers to oversee the election, voiced grave doubts about security in parts of the country.
Tensions have been mounting across Albania in the run-up to the election, with political and administrative control lax and some areas controlled by gangs.
But a state of emergency imposed in March by the interim national unity government has eased: a nightly curfew now falls at 10 p.m., an hour later than last week.
The government has also said there will be no curfew on polling day itself, meeting fears among opposition parties and the OSCE that this could obscure the election outcome.

Nonetheless, the 100 or so OSCE observers already in the country need protection from a 6,500-strong Italian-led multinational protection force to travel. Some have not yet been able to reach areas they were due to visit last week.

Italy is planning to send more troops, and the multinational force's steering committee meets in Rome on Tuesday to decide on beefing it up and extending its mandate, which is currently due to expire a day before the poll.
"(The observers) are going to go everywhere that the multinational protection force can provide an escort for them," Jeff Murray, OSCE spokesman, told Reuters in Tirana.
